growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays in the soil and first drives down a taproot (about 70 cm in 2 months). The shoot is a thin, reddish, downy stem with small, cupped, glossy, spiny-toothed evergreen leaves. Seedlings grow slowly in the shade of shrubs or grass for years, then form a slender sapling before spreading into a broad dome; it resprouts strongly after fire.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Quercus agrifolia (acorns germinate 15-50 d after falling, no dormancy; taproot ~70 cm in 2 months; slow natural top growth; recruitment best in shade; shade tolerant throughout life; 6-25 m; trees may live over 250 yr); first acorn age estimated

Within a few years the bark begins thickening into pale, spongy, deeply fissured cork. Saplings grow best sheltered by shrubs but need more light later; the first 'virgin' cork is stripped when the tree is about 25 years old.
growth.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (Quercus suber: usually 20 m, to 25 m; slow-growing; about 200 yr or more); Wikipedia (10-15 m typical; first cork harvest at ~25 yr, then every 9-12 yr; trees can live over 400 yr); growth curve, shade and first acorns estimated

fruiting.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (flowers from April through summer; both annual and biennial acorns, 2-3 cm, fairly deep cup with long scales); Wikipedia (acorns 2-4.5 cm, bare, smooth, shiny brownish-red; 15-30 kg of acorns per tree per year)

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays buried and roots deeply before a thin shoot appears. Seedlings and saplings carry holly-like leaves with spiny teeth, dark glossy green above and grey-felted below; adult leaves are smaller, entire and leathery. Young plants grow slowly in the shade of shrubs and trees, often bushy from browsing, before a single stem leads.
growth.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (Quercus ilex: to 25 m, rarely 30; lifespan may exceed 1000 yr; shade-tolerant, regenerates under canopy); Wikipedia (young trees spiny-toothed, adults entire; Encina Tres Patas ~1,200 yr); growth rate and first-acorn age estimated

fruiting.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (flowers May-Jun with new leaves; acorns ripen the first year, brown, 1.5-2 cm, a third to half in a light green cup; fall Nov-Jan; big crops every 4-6 yr); Wikipedia (1-3 acorns on a short stalk); sweet acorns of subsp. rotundifolia are eaten raw or roasted

canopy.name: Mediterranean cypress

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal, with slender cotyledons; the first shoots bear small, spreading needle-like juvenile leaves before the dark green, appressed scale leaves take over. Fast-growing when young: a dense, narrow cone of upswept branches (a slim column in the fastigiate form, which is what most planted trees are; wild trees spread horizontally).
growth.source: conifers.org (20-30 m, fast-growing when young, seeds from its tenth year, up to 1000 yr; cones 2-3 cm, 8-14 scales, serotinous); Wikipedia (to 35 m, >1000 yr, Sarv-e Abarkuh estimated ~4000 yr); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (cones ripen second year, 64-280 seeds, 28-d germination test)

canopy.source: E Mediterranean hills; the dark column of graveyards and ruins. Kew POWO.

Adult paired, stiff green needles gradually take over by about age 10; the tree then lifts into a flat umbrella crown on a bare trunk.
growth.source: Wikipedia (juvenile leaves for 5-10 years, fully adult by ~10; a bushy globe in youth, an umbrella in mid-age; 12-20 m typical, to 25+; cones take 36 months to mature, longest of any pine); first cones and lifespan estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval cotyledons, then pairs of small, short, rounded-oval leaves, much less narrow than the adult's. The young wild olive is a dense, twiggy, often spiny shrub of many stems with tiny leaves (a browse-resistant juvenile form) for years; eventually one or a few stems grow out into a tree with narrow, grey-green, silver-backed leaves and a gnarled, fissured, hollowing trunk.
growth.source: Olive horticulture and oleaster ecology: long juvenile phase (seedlings fruit after ~8-15 yr), juvenile foliage small and rounded with spiny shoots; seed with hard endocarp germinates slowly (1-6 months after removal of the stone); trees live many centuries, some over 2000 yr (Wikipedia Olive; Rey & Alcantara 2000 on oleaster recruitment)

fruiting.source: Olive crop literature (Lavee; FAO/IOC): small creamy 4-lobed flowers in axillary racemes of 10-40 in spring, mainly wind pollinated, only ~1-2% of flowers set fruit; fruit green turning purple-black in autumn-winter, ~5-7 months after bloom; wild oleaster fruit small (~1-1.5 cm); bitter until cured

growth.juvenile_note: After a fire, seedlings come up en masse with the first winter rains: two small round cotyledons, then stiff, pale blue-grey, round-oval leaves held edge-on to the sun on a single reddish stem. It branches into a bushy rounded shrub, and the smooth red-purple bark and twisting limbs of the adult show within a few years. It has no burl, so fire kills it.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Arctostaphylos glauca: shrub 1 to over 6 m; seeds need fire to germinate; long-lived, 100+ yr, but does not fruit until about 20 yr old; reproduces by seed and layering). Chaparral seedling ecology from USDA FEIS (Arctostaphylos glandulosa). Germination days and height-age estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (hanging clusters of narrow urn-shaped white flowers; drupe 12-15 mm, light red, thick pulp in a tough sticky coat, 3-6 nutlets fused into one stone; eaten and made into cider). Winter flowering months, pollinators (bees, hummingbirds), timings and crop estimated from Jepson as recalled and FEIS manzanita accounts.

Most young plants seen are resprouts instead: dozens (up to 500) of straight, wand-like green shoots from the burned burl, about 50 cm tall after one season.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Adenostoma fasciculatum (heat- and charate-stimulated germination in the first rainy season after fire; ~90% first-year seedling mortality; seed by ~3 yr; sprouts 50 cm yr 1, 85 cm yr 5, 1 m yr 20; lives 100-200 yr; shade intolerant)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Adenostoma fasciculatum (white flowers in showy 2.5-10 cm terminal clusters on current growth in June; fruit develops in July; ripening and dispersal complete by August; achenes; seed output rises with shrub age); pollinators estimated (generalist insects)

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds wait in the soil until fire or summer heat cracks them; seedlings flood in with the autumn rains. Two small oval cotyledons, then pairs of narrow lance-shaped leaves, dark green and glossy-sticky above with fragrant labdanum resin. It becomes an erect, open, few-stemmed shrub and flowers within 2-3 years.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cistus ladanifer (1-2.5 m, flowers 5-8 cm with 5 white papery petals, sticky leaves 3-10 cm); Talavera et al. 1993 and Narbona et al. studies (flowers last one day, bee- and beetle-pollinated, many-valved capsules with ~1000 seeds; heat-stimulated germination; stands senesce after ~20-30 yr)

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (white 5-8 cm flowers, petals often with a maroon blotch); Talavera, Gibbs & Herrera 1993 (Cistus ladanifer: one-day flowers, self-incompatible, pollinated by bees and beetles, globose capsules with ~10 valves opening slowly from late summer, seeds released over months)

The young plant stays a low, dense, prickly bush; a woody root crown and spreading roots throw up many suckers, so it becomes a thicket (garrigue) that resprouts within weeks after fire, cutting or grazing.

Leaves wither in the summer drought and regrow each autumn; after 2-4 years the clump sends up a branched spike of white, brown-veined star flowers.
